Back to [session 11](../sessions/11-glmm.qmd).

## The data

Mothers' behaviour towards their infants changes as the infants grow up. In this practical, you analyse how often **wild Guinea baboon infants receive approaches from their mothers** over the first 18 months of life.

::: {.box-warn}
The data are **simulated**; their structure is modelled on Dal Pesco et al. (2026). Each row is one infant in one month: focal observation time (`hours`) differs between rows, and most infants are observed in several months.
:::

[Download `simulated_baboons.csv`](../../data/simulated_baboons.csv){download="simulated_baboons.csv"}

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `infant` | infant ID |
| `age.months` | infant age in months |
| `sex` | infant sex (F, M) |
| `hours` | focal observation time in this month (hours) |
| `z.age` | age, z-transformed |
| `approaches` | number of approaches received from the mother |

: {.striped}




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# adjust the path to where you saved the file
xdata <- read.csv("../../data/simulated_baboons.csv")
xdata$sex <- factor(xdata$sex)
```
:::




## Exercise 1: explore the data

How many rows and how many infants are there? How many months is each infant observed? Plot the **rate** of approaches (per hour) against age, with one line per infant.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(xdata)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 548
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
length(unique(xdata$infant))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 80
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(as.vector(table(xdata$infant)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    4.00    5.00    7.00    6.85    8.00   10.00
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
xdata$rate <- xdata$approaches / xdata$hours
ggplot(xdata, aes(age.months, rate, group = infant)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .3, colour = "#1b6f8a") +
  labs(x = "Age (months)", y = "Approaches per hour")
```

About 550 rows from 80 infants: each infant contributes several rows, so the rows are **not independent**.
:::

## Exercise 2: the model we already know

Fit a Poisson GLM of `approaches` with `z.age` and `sex` as predictors. Why do you need an **offset**, and what does it look like? Interpret the age effect on the response scale.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
glm.mod <- glm(approaches ~ z.age + sex + offset(log(hours)),
               family = poisson, data = xdata)
summary(glm.mod)$coefficients
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -0.07007817 0.06797552 -1.030932 3.025725e-01
#> z.age       -0.53211214 0.05422193 -9.813596 9.839836e-23
#> sexM         0.26284398 0.08496598  3.093520 1.977971e-03
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
exp(coef(glm.mod)["z.age"])       # multiplicative change in the rate per SD of age
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     z.age 
#> 0.5873631
```


:::
:::




Observation time differs between rows, so we model the **rate** of approaches. With a log link, `offset(log(hours))` does this without estimating an extra parameter (see [offset](../../glossary.qmd#offset)). The rate of approaches changes by the factor shown above per SD of age (about 5 months).
:::

## Exercise 3: add a random intercept

Fit the same model with a random intercept for `infant`. Compare the standard errors of `z.age` and `sex` with those of the GLM. What does the random-intercept SD tell you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ri.mod <- glmer(approaches ~ z.age + sex + offset(log(hours)) + (1 | infant),
                family = poisson, data = xdata,
                control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

se <- function(m) sqrt(diag(vcov(m)))[c("z.age", "sexM")]
round(rbind(GLM = se(glm.mod), GLMM = se(ri.mod)), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      z.age  sexM
#> GLM  0.054 0.085
#> GLMM 0.077 0.188
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
VarCorr(ri.mod)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>  Groups Name        Std.Dev.
#>  infant (Intercept) 0.69112
```


:::
:::




The standard error of `sex` is much larger in the GLMM: sex varies **between** infants, so the effective sample size for it is the number of infants, not the number of rows. The SD of the random intercept says how much infants differ in their baseline rate (on the log scale).
:::

## Exercise 4: add a random slope

Infants may differ not only in their baseline, but also in how the rate changes with age. Add a random slope for `z.age`. Use `(1 + z.age || infant)`, which leaves out the correlation between intercept and slope. Compare the confidence interval of the age effect with the previous models.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rs.mod <- glmer(approaches ~ z.age + sex + offset(log(hours)) + (1 + z.age || infant),
                family = poisson, data = xdata,
                control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
VarCorr(rs.mod)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>  Groups   Name        Std.Dev.
#>  infant   (Intercept) 0.65406 
#>  infant.1 z.age       0.27426
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ci <- function(m) {                       # Wald 95% CI for z.age
  cf <- summary(m)$coefficients["z.age", ]
  c(lower = cf[[1]] - 1.96 * cf[[2]], upper = cf[[1]] + 1.96 * cf[[2]])
}
round(rbind(GLM = ci(glm.mod), `GLMM (1 | infant)` = ci(ri.mod),
            `GLMM (1 + z.age || infant)` = ci(rs.mod)), 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                             lower  upper
#> GLM                        -0.638 -0.426
#> GLMM (1 | infant)          -0.543 -0.242
#> GLMM (1 + z.age || infant) -0.479 -0.122
```


:::
:::




`z.age` varies **within** infants, and infants differ in their age slopes. Only the model with the random slope reflects this, and its confidence interval for the age effect is wider. Leaving out the random slope makes the test of age too liberal. (Compare with the true value in Exercise 7: the GLM interval does not even contain it.)
:::

## Exercise 5: test the effect of sex

Test whether sex affects the rate of approaches with a likelihood-ratio test. Keep the random-effects structure in both models.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rs.null <- glmer(approaches ~ z.age + offset(log(hours)) + (1 + z.age || infant),
                 family = poisson, data = xdata,
                 control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
anova(rs.null, rs.mod)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> Data: xdata
#> Models:
#> rs.null: approaches ~ z.age + offset(log(hours)) + (1 + z.age || infant)
#> rs.mod: approaches ~ z.age + sex + offset(log(hours)) + (1 + z.age || infant)
#>         npar    AIC    BIC  logLik deviance  Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)
#> rs.null    4 1320.5 1337.8 -656.27   1312.5                     
#> rs.mod     5 1322.0 1343.6 -656.01   1312.0 0.5064  1     0.4767
```


:::
:::




No evidence for a sex effect. Compare this with the GLM from Exercise 2, which reports a "significant" sex effect: sex varies only between infants, and the GLM treats the ~550 rows as independent ([pseudoreplication](../../glossary.qmd#pseudoreplication)).
:::

## Exercise 6: plot the result

Plot the model-predicted rate of approaches over age: one line per infant, plus the population-average line.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nd <- unique(xdata[, c("infant", "sex", "age.months", "z.age")])
nd$hours <- 1                                                        # rate per hour
nd$p_inf <- predict(rs.mod, newdata = nd, type = "response")
avg <- data.frame(age.months = 0:18, sex = "F", hours = 1)
avg$z.age <- (avg$age.months - 9) / 5.2
avg$p <- predict(rs.mod, newdata = avg, type = "response", re.form = NA)  # without random effects

ggplot(nd, aes(age.months, p_inf, group = infant)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .25, colour = "#1b6f8a") +
  geom_line(data = avg, aes(age.months, p), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#c0392b", linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "Age (months)", y = "Predicted approaches per hour",
       caption = "Blue: infants · red: average female infant")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](11-glmm_files/figure-html/ex6-1.png){width=975}
:::
:::

## Exercise 7: report

Write two or three sentences reporting the age and sex effects as you would in a paper. Include the model, effect sizes on the response scale, and the test results.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Check the truth"}
The data were simulated with an age effect of −0.3 (log scale, per SD of age), **no** sex effect, an SD of 0.6 for the random intercept and an SD of 0.25 for the random age slope. How close did your model get?
:::
